text: Kururunfa is an advanced kata traditionally attributed to Goju-Ryu. According to tradition, Kanryō Higaonna brought it from Fuzhou (Southern China), but there are very few historical records. Researcher Akio Kinjo suggests that Kururunfa may be related to Chinese Palongfa (臥龍法), "lying dragon technique", but this remains speculative. The kata is certainly effective, short and fast; against Higaonna's usual hard blocks, Kururunfa is executed sharply. It may also be that Miyagi Chōjun composed Kururunfa himself from techniques he learned in China and Okinawa. The fact remains that Kururunfa is not widely found in other styles and is typical of the traditional Goju-ryu lineage.

text: Miyagi Sensei apparently learned Kururunfa in the tradition of Higaonna (or via his own Chinese journey). He introduced it as an advanced kata, which showed that Higaonna (or Miyagi) had brought more than just the four classical kata (Sanchin, Sanseiru, Seisan, Suparinpei). In any case, Kururunfa remained in the Goju line: later Goju masters (e.g., Miyazato, Higaonna Morio) have maintained it. Mas Oyama included Kururunfa – like Tensho – in Kyokushin via Gogen Yamaguchi, which also made it known in Kyokushin circles.

text: Kururunfa has always remained a complex kata within Goju and underwent little change. The form is completely different from the earlier kata; there are no "simpler versions". However, there is some difference in emphasis: some schools emphasize Tai Sabaki (upper body movements) with each strike, others focus slightly less on those body points. Importantly, Kururunfa at the time – unlike the other five hard kata – is executed in one smooth movement, which aligns with Higaonna's concept of 'slip-, step- and away'-technique (zenshin). There are no major controversies about the kata: it is simply passed on as Miyagi left it.

text: Kururunfa combines flowing circular movements with sudden outbursts. After a calm, stable start, the fist is launched with a built-in "slip, slide" tactic. Typical applications in the kata are (in bunkai) counter-knees to the thigh (tobi-hiza), kakate hand grips (hook grips to unbalance the opponent), palm strikes and arm locks. Philosophically, Kururunfa teaches distance control: one remains calm until the opponent exposes themselves, then uses rapid evasion combined with – via hook grips – a rotation for a finishing strike or throw. The kata is very "internal" in the sense that one controls energy (Qi) through body efficiency; deep breathing and rapid rotations play a major role.

text: Kururunfa is often considered strongly influenced by Southern Chinese snake or dragon styles. Akio Kinjo mentioned parallels with Fujianese "lying dragon" principles. Links with Mantis (Cricket) have also been suggested, due to the emphasis on rapid hip movements and low strikes. The name also suggests kinship with Saifa (the sister kata "tearing and destroying" from the south) through the use of "fa" (破) in both names. In summary, Kururunfa is a kata that stands in the tradition of Naha-te, but in execution has much in common with southern Chinese arts.

text: Kururunfa (来留蹲破 according to some writers) is often explained as "standing still, then suddenly striking" or "slowly holding, suddenly destroying". The name is broken down: Ku (long or always), ru (holding or staying calm), run (suddenly) and fa (tearing, breaking). So Kururunfa can literally mean "always still, suddenly breaking". Another approach is "maintain your patience, then suddenly enter". This reinforces the essence: remaining calm in anticipation of an attack, then striking with lightning speed in one movement.
